fields.title: Men of Prayer
fields.description: Men of Prayer: Fifteen Voices That Changed the World calls pastors, teachers, and Christian leaders in Uganda back to the secret place of power. Through the lives of fifteen men whose prayers shaped history, this book reveals how God works through humble and persistent intercession.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
A Fire That Must Not Die

Prayer is the heartbeat of the Church. Wherever God has moved powerfully in history — wherever the Gospel has broken open hard ground, wherever revivals have swept nations, wherever the darkness has retreated before the light of Christ — there has always been a company of men and women who refused to stop praying. They prayed in the dawn hours before their families woke. They prayed through the night when armies threatened and nations hung in the balance. They prayed for the lost, for the sick, for the broken, for the church, and for the glory of God. And God answered.

This book is about fifteen such men. They span four centuries, five continents, and many different Christian traditions. Some were scholars; others had little formal education. Some pastored great congregations in famous cities; others ministered in obscurity to small flocks in remote places. Some are well known to the global church; others are known mainly by those who search deeply for great examples of prayer. But they all share one thing in common: they were men who prayed, and because they prayed, the world was changed.

Why This Book is for Ugandan Pastors

Uganda is a nation with a remarkable Christian heritage. The Uganda Martyrs — those young men who died for Christ in 1886 rather than deny their Lord — sealed the Church of Uganda with the blood of the saints. The East African Revival of the 1930s and 1940s transformed thousands of lives across Uganda and neighbouring nations, and its fruit is still visible today.

Uganda has been described by many as one of the most prayerful nations on earth.

Yet every generation must discover prayer for itself. It is not enough to inherit the prayers of our fathers. Each pastor, each elder, each teacher, each church leader must come before God in their own name, with their own burdens, and learn to pray with their own voice. The fire on the altar must be kept burning. It must be fed with fresh wood every morning.

This book is written for Ugandan pastors and teachers because the responsibility of a pastor is unique. You carry the burden of your congregation on your shoulders. You preach on Sundays, counsel the grieving, visit the sick, train young believers, and lead your church in worship. You face opposition, discouragement, poverty, and sometimes betrayal. You need the power of prayer more than any other person in your community. If you do not pray, your words become hollow, your counsel becomes mere advice, and your ministry becomes mere activity. But if you pray — if you learn to meet God in the secret place every day — then everything you do will carry the weight of heaven.

About These Fifteen Men

The fifteen men in this book were chosen because they represent the full breadth of what prayer looks like in a devoted life. They include: • Andrew Murray — the South African Dutch Reformed pastor who wrote more than 200 books on the deeper life and prayer • Charles Spurgeon — the Prince of Preachers, whose Metropolitan Tabernacle was built and sustained through prayer • Watchman Nee — the Chinese church planter who spent the last twenty years of his life in a Communist prison for his faith • D. L. Moody — the uneducated shoe salesman who became the greatest evangelist of the nineteenth century • A. R. Torrey — Moody's successor, whose book How to Pray remains one of the most practical guides to prayer ever written • E. M. Bounds — who prayed from four to seven in the morning every day, and whose eight books on prayer were all published after his death • Jonathan Edwards — the Puritan theologian whose preaching and prayers helped ignite the First Great Awakening in America • Charles Finney — the revivalist lawyer whose prayer-soaked ministry saw over half a million people come to Christ • Rees Howells — the Welsh intercessor whose prayer group is credited with turning the tide of World War II through intercession • Billy Graham — who preached the Gospel to more people face to face than anyone in history • Henry Blackaby — whose Experiencing God has taught millions to hear and obey the voice of God in prayer • Bill Bright — who founded Campus Crusade for Christ and whose Jesus film has been seen by over five billion people • Loren Cunningham — founder of Youth With A Mission, who received his entire vision for world evangelism through prayer • Derek Prince — the Cambridge scholar who was converted reading a Bible alone in a military barracks and spent sixty years teaching on prayer and spiritual warfare • Timothy Keller — the pastor who planted Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan and helped the global church understand prayer as awe, intimacy, and encounter with the living God How This Book is Organised Each chapter covers one man. You will find: 1. A short biography — who he was, where he came from, and what he accomplished 2. A great answer to prayer from his life — a specific story showing that God truly hears and answers 3. Key scriptures — two or three Bible passages most connected to his life and teaching on prayer 4. His words on prayer — five powerful quotes showing how he understood and practised prayer 5. Prayer and the Word of God — how he connected prayer with Scripture 6. Prayer and the Holy Spirit — how he understood the Spirit's role in prayer A Word Before You Begin This book is designed to be used, not simply read. Each chapter can serve as the basis for a personal study day, a prayer meeting, a sermon, a pastors' retreat, or a discipleship conversation.

The quotes are suitable for preaching. The biographies and answered prayers are suitable for teaching. The scriptures anchor everything in the Word of God.

Do not rush through this book. Sit with each man for a while. Let his life challenge you. Let his words stir your hunger. Let his answered prayer build your faith. And then go and pray.

As Andrew Murray wrote: “The man who mobilises the Christian church to pray will make the greatest contribution to world evangelisation in history.” Uganda needs men and women like that. Perhaps you are one of them.

Read. Be stirred. Pray. Change the world.

fields.title: Andrew Murray (1828 – 1917)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Andrew Murray was born on 9 May 1828 in Graaff Reinet, South Africa, the son of a Dutch Reformed Church missionary from Scotland. When he was ten years old, he and his brother John were sent to Scotland for their education, where they were deeply influenced by revivalist preachers like William Burns. They went on to study theology at the University of Utrecht in Holland, where they resisted the rationalism of the day and formed a small prayer group known mockingly as the “Chocolate Club.”

Ordained in 1848, Murray was given the enormous task of being the only minister over a 50,000-square-mile territory in remote South Africa. For weeks at a time he would ride on horseback to preach to isolated Dutch-speaking farming families. He married Emma Rutherford in 1856 and together they had eight children.

Murray pastored churches in Bloemfontein, Worcester, Cape Town, and Wellington over his long ministry, and became the central figure in the South African Revival of 1860. In 1879 he lost his voice entirely for two years due to a throat condition — a season of suffering that drove him deeper into prayer and the study of Scripture. Following a miraculous healing in London in 1881, he emerged with an even more fervent dedication to God.

Over the remaining decades of his life, Murray wrote more than 240 books and tracts, including the timeless classics Abide in Christ, Humility, and With Christ in the School of Prayer. His books have been translated into dozens of languages and continue to be read by millions. He died on 18 January 1917 at the age of 88, having shaped the global church's understanding of prayer, the Holy Spirit, and the deeper Christian life more profoundly than almost any writer of his era.

A Great Answer to Prayer

For more than thirty years, Murray's father had prayed every Friday evening for revival to come to South Africa. He would read revival accounts to his family and then retire to his study to pour out his heart to God. The son grew up watching this, and the hunger for revival was instilled in him from childhood.

In May 1860, Andrew Murray was newly installed as pastor in Worcester when a conference on revival was convened. As speakers told of revivals in America and Europe, the congregation began to hunger. One evening, without any premeditation, the entire congregation spontaneously began weeping and crying out to God — hundreds of voices simultaneously, men and women, young and old, overflowing with prayer and confession.

Murray initially resisted, calling for order and silence. But his father came and told him, “Andrew, my son, I have longed for such times as these, which the Lord has let you have.”

Murray realised this was the revival his father had prayed for over three decades. He surrendered and embraced what God was doing. The revival spread throughout the whole country and bore lasting fruit — a direct answer to those thirty years of faithful, quiet, persistent prayer.

Later in life, Murray's two-year loss of voice was itself followed by a dramatic answer to prayer.

When all medical remedies failed, he travelled to Bethshan, a faith home in London, where he was completely and instantly healed through prayer and faith. He never again suffered from throat trouble and went on to write and preach for another thirty-six years.

Key Scriptures

John 15:7 — “If you abide in Me, and My words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.”

Ephesians 6:18 — “Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication.

To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is not merely coming to God to ask something of Hi m. It is, above all, fellowship with God and being brought under the power of His holiness and love, until He takes possession of us and stamps our entire nature with the lowliness of Christ, which is the secret of all true worship.”

“Prayer is not monolo gue, but dialogue; God's voice is its most essential part. Listening to God's voice is the secret of the assurance that He will listen to mine.”

“Time spent in prayer will yield more than that given to work. Prayer alone gives work its worth and its success. Prayer opens the way for God Himself to do His work in us and through us.”

“The Holy Spirit comes in answer to believing prayer. The measure of believing, continued prayer will be the measure of the Spirit's working in the Church.”

“Nothing so reveal s a defective spiritual life in a minister or a congregation as the lack of believing and unceasing prayer. Prayer is the pulse of the spiritual life. It is the great means by which ministers and laypeople alike receive the blessing and power of heaven.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Many do not understand this union of the teaching of the Word and the Spirit, so there is a twofold difficulty in knowing what God's will may be. Some seek the will of God in an inner feeling or conviction and would have the Spirit lead them without the Word. Others seek it in the Word without the leading of the Holy Spirit. The two must be united — the Word and the Spirit — because only in these can we know for sure the will of God and learn to pray according to it.”

“A readine ss to believe every promise implicitly, to obey every command unhesitatingly, to stand perfect and complete in all the will of God, is the only true spirit of Bible study.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“In every prayer the triune God takes a part — the Father who hears, the Son in whose name we pray, and the Spirit who prays for us and in us. How important it is that we are in right relationship to the Holy Spirit and that we understand His work!”

“Through His Spirit, the Spirit of prayer, our life may be o ne of continual prayer. The Spirit of prayer will help you become an intercessor, asking great things of God for those around you.”

“If the spiritual life be healthy, under the full power of the Holy Spirit, praying without ceasing will be natural.”

fields.title: Charles Spurgeon (1834 – 1892)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Charles Haddon Spurgeon was born on 19 June 1834 in Kelvedon, Essex, England, into a family of preachers — both his father and grandfather were Congregationalist ministers. He was dramatically converted at the age of sixteen when, caught in a snowstorm, he stumbled into a small Primitive Methodist chapel and heard a lay preacher speak on Isaiah 45:22: “Look unto Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.” The simple message pierced his heart and he was born again.

Within the year he was installed as pastor of a small Baptist congregation, and by the age of twenty he had been called to New Park Street Chapel in London — one of the most significant Baptist churches in the country. His preaching immediately drew enormous crowds. The chapel was far too small, and after moving to several larger venues, the Metropolitan Tabernacle was built in 1861 to seat 6,000 people.

Spurgeon preached to an estimated ten million people over his lifetime, trained nearly nine hundr ed pastors through his Pastors’ College, founded an orphanage, and wrote prolifically — his collected sermons filling sixty-three volumes and still being read today. He preached typically four times a week and knew his 6,000 members by name.

Despite his extraordinary ministry, Spurgeon suffered greatly from gout, depression, and the grief of false accusations from fellow ministers. He never ceased preaching through his suffering, and many of his deepest writings on prayer came from his darkest seasons. He died in Menton, France, on 31 January 1892, aged 57, and is still widely regarded as the greatest preacher of the modern era.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Early in his ministry at New Park Street Chapel, Spurgeon faced a crisis of faith. The congregation was small and declining. He prayed earnestly for God to fill the church with souls.

Within months of his arrival, the building was overflowing, the aisles jammed, and thousands stood outside straining to hear. Spurgeon testified that this dramatic turnaround was purely and entirely an answer to prayer.

More profoundly, Spurgeon often spoke of the prayer meeting as the engine of Metropolitan Tabernacle. He said the Monday evening prayer meeting — attended by thousands every week — was the secret of everything the Tabernacle accomplished. When asked about the power of his ministry, he would take visitors to the basement where hundreds of people could be found on their knees at any hour. “Here,” he said, “is the powerhouse.”

One of the most celebrated stories in Spurgeon's ministry involves a bedridden woman who read of D.L. Moody's meetings in America. She began praying specifically for God to send a great preacher to her own church in London. Unknown to her, Moody arrived in England and was invited — by the pastor of her very congregation — to preach. The result was extraordinary — hundreds coming to faith in a single meeting. Spurgeon used this story repeatedly to demonstrate the power of one praying person.

Key Scriptures

Jeremiah 33:3 — “Call to Me and I will answer you, and I will tell you great and mighty things, which you do not know.”

Hebrews 4:16 — “Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need.”

Matthew 21:22 — “And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.”

His Words on Prayer

“True prayer is measured by weight, not by length. A single groan before God may have more fullness of prayer in it than a fine oration of great length.”

“Prayer is the slender nerve that moves the muscle of omnipotence.”

“The power of prayer can never be overrated. They who cannot serve God by preaching need not regret. If a man can but pray, he can do anything. He who knows how to overcome with God in prayer has Heaven and earth at hi s disposal.”

“After all, prayer is nothing but taking God's promises to Him, and saying to Him, “Do as Thou hast said.” Prayer is the promise utilised. A prayer which is not based on a promise has no true foundation.”

“In prayer, we stand where angels bo w with veiled faces. There, even there, the cherubim and seraphim adore before that selfsame throne to which our prayers ascend. And shall we come there with stunted requests and narrow, contracted faith?”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Whenever you cannot u nderstand a text, open your Bible, bend your knee, and pray over that text. Prayer is the key that opens the cabinets of mystery. Prayer and faith are sacred picklocks that can open secrets and obtain great treasures.”

“The best praying man is the man who is most believingly familiar with the promises of God. After all, prayer is nothing but taking God's promises to Him, and saying to Him, “Do as Thou hast said.””

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Prayer is the creation of the Holy Spirit. We cannot do without prayer, and we cannot pray without the Holy Spirit.”

“If you could pray the best prayer in the world without the Holy Spirit, God would have nothing to do with it. But if your prayer be broken and lame and limping, if the Spirit made it, God will look upo n it and say, as He did upon the works of creation, “It is very good.””

“Prayer is the autograph of the Holy Ghost upon the renewed heart.”

fields.title: Watchman Nee (1903 – 1972)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Watchman Nee — whose Chinese name was Ni To-sheng, meaning “ringing bell” — was born in Foochow, China, in 1903, into a third-generation Christian family. His grandfather had been the first Chinese Congregationalist pastor in Fujian province, and his mother prayed for a son before Watchman was born, promising to give him to God. He was saved at the age of seventeen, in 1920, through the ministry of the evangelist Dora Yu.

Within three years of his conversion, Watchman was writing and publishing theological journals, preaching across China, and planting what he called “local churches” — congregations rooted in the New Testament pattern and not dependent on Western denominational structures. By 1932, these local churches had spread throughout China, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore.

He published his landmark three-volume work The Spiritual Man in 1928, and his best-known book The Normal Christian Life — one of the great classics of Christian literature — was based on talks he gave in English during his travels in Europe in 1938 and 1939.

In 1952, the Communist government arrested Watchman Nee for his faith. After a long trial, he was sentenced in 1956 to fifteen years’ imprisonment, but was never released. He spent the final twenty years of his life in prison, and died there on 30 May 1972. When he died, a small piece of pa per was found under his pillow. It read: “Christ is the Son of God who died for the redemption of sinners and was resurrected after three days. This is the greatest truth in the universe. I die because of my belief in Christ.”

A Great Answer to Prayer

During an evangelistic mission to Mei-hua Island off the South China coast, Watchman Nee and a small team of young believers encountered fierce opposition from idol worshippers. A local festival to the idol Ta-wang was approaching, and the idol’s devotees dec lared confidently that their god would send clear weather for the procession day — implying that if Nee’s God was real, He should demonstrate power.

Nee and his team prayed. On the morning of the festival, as they were saying grace for breakfast, rain began to fall — light at first, then torrential. The idol’s carriers struggled to carry it in procession and stumbled, dropping it and fracturing its jaw and arm. The power of the idol over the island was broken. A number of young people turned to Christ immediately.

The elders of the village declared that the wrong day had been chosen, and announced a new procession day: the fourteenth. Nee and his team prayed again, asking for clear weather between the two dates for preaching, and for rain again on the fourteenth. God answered precisely: clear days for preaching produced thirty converts, and then, exactly on the fourteenth, torrential rain fell at the appointed hour. Nee recorded: “We quietly brought the matter to the Lord’s remembrance. Not a minute late, His answer came with torrential rain and floods as before. The power of the idol over the islanders was broken; the enemy was defeated. Believing prayer had brought a great victory.”

Key Scriptures

Romans 8:26 – 27 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For w e do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.”

1 John 5:14 – 15 — “This is the confidence that we have toward Him, that if we ask anything according to His will He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of Him.”

Ephesians 6:18 — “Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication.”

His Words on Prayer

“Our prayers lay the track down which G od's power can come. Like a mighty locomotive, His power is irresistible, but it cannot reach us without rails.”

“The purpose of prayer is not to notify God but to express our trust, our faith, our expectation, and our heart desire.”

“Negligence in praye r withers the inner man. Nothing can be a substitute for it, not even Christian work. Prayer enables us first inwardly to overcome the enemy and then outwardly to deal with him.”

“Prayer is the acid test of the inner man's strength. A strong spirit is cap able of praying much and praying with all perseverance until the answer comes.”

“Let us recognise this one thing: burden is the secret of prayer. If a person does not feel within him burden to pray for a particular matter, he can hardly succeed in prayer. ” Prayer and the Word of God “We should not open our mouths too hastily upon approaching God. On the contrary, we first must ask God to show us what and how to pray before we make our request known to Him. Have we not consumed a great deal of time in the past asking for what we wanted?

Why not now ask for what God wants?”

“Prayer according to the will of God is only possible when we ourselves are in harmony with His will.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Prayer is work. The experiences of many children of Go d demonstrate that it accomplishes far more than does any other form of work. It is also warfare, for it is one of the weapons in fighting the enemy. However, only prayer in the Spirit is genuinely effectual.”

“The burden imparted by God is lifted once we have prayed, but the heaviness from the enemy cannot be raised unless we fight and resist in prayer.”

“Why do so many Christians pray such tiny prayers when their God is so big?”

fields.title: D. L. Moody (1837 – 1899)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Dwight Lyman Moody was born on 5 February 1837 in Northfield, Massachusetts, the sixth of nine children. His father died when he was four, leaving the family in poverty. He received only a fifth-grade education and moved to Boston at seventeen to work in his uncle’s shoe store. He was converted in 1855 at the age of eighteen, when his Sunday school teacher Edward Kimball came to the shoe store and led him to Christ behind the counter.

Moving to Chicago, Moody threw himself into Christian work — the YMCA, a Sunday school for the poor children of the slums, and an independent church that grew into a congregation of 1,500. He was a man of enormous energy, warmth, and practical love. After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed his church building, he was left with nothing — but what followed was a crisis of prayer that transformed him.

In 1871, while in New York seeking funds to rebuild, Moody was walking down a street when the power of the Holy Spirit fell on him so overwhelmingly that he had to ask God to stop. His preaching immediately changed in power and effect, and hundreds were converted wherever he went. From that point he became the greatest mass evangelist of the nineteenth century.

Together with singer Ira Sankey, Moody conducted crusades across America and Great Britain that became defining moments in evangelical history. He founded the Moody Bible Institute in Chicago in 1889, the Northfield Schools in Massachusetts, and a publishing house that still bears his name. It is estimated that he preached to over 100 million people in his lifetime. He died on 22 December 1899 and was buried in his hometown of Northfield.

A Great Answer to Prayer

After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 consumed his church and most of his ministry’s physical foundations, Moody was broken. Two women in his congregation had been telling him for months about the need for the filling of the Holy Spirit. He had brushed them aside. Now, stripped of everything, he began to pray desperately.

While walking the streets of New York raising money for a new building, God met him. Moody himself described it: “I was crying all the time that God would fill me with His Spirit. Well, one day in the city of New York — oh, what a day! — I cannot describe it, I seldom refer to it; it is almost too sacred an experience to name. I can only say that God revealed Himself to me, and I had such an experience of His love that I had to ask Him to stay His hand. I went to preaching again. The sermons were not different; I did not present any new truths; and yet hundreds were converted. I would not be placed back where I was before that blessed experience for all the world.”

The fire of God had fallen in answer to prayer. Moody went on from that moment to preach the Gospel to millions, fill the largest arenas in America and Britain, and change the course of evangelical Christianity worldwide.

Key Scriptures

Romans 10:17 — “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of Christ.”

Acts 1:8 — “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

Matthew 9:37 – 38 — “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into His harvest.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer does not mean that I am to bring God down to my thoughts and my purposes, and bend His government according to my foolish, silly, and sometimes sinful notions.

Prayer means that I am to be raised up into feeling, into union and design with Him; that I am to enter into His counsel and carry out His purpose fully.”

“In our prayers, we talk to God; in our Bible study, God talks to us; and we had better let God do most of the talking.”

“I would rather be able to pray than to be a great pr eacher; Jesus Christ never taught His disciples how to preach, but only how to pray.”

“Next to the wonder of seeing my Saviour will be, I think, the wonder that I made so little use of the power of prayer.”

“The Christian on his knees sees more than the philosopher on tiptoe. God sends no one away empty except those who are full of themselves.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“I prayed for faith, and thought that some day faith would come down and strike me like lightning. But faith did not seem to come. One day I read in the tenth chapter of Romans, “Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God.” I had closed my Bible and prayed for faith. I now opened my Bible and began to study, and faith has been growing ever since.”

“One thing I have noticed i n studying the Word of God: when a man is filled with the Spirit, he deals largely with the Word of God; whereas the man who is filled with his own ideas refers rarely to the Word of God.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“The Bible without the Holy Spirit is a sundial by moonlight.”

“I believe firmly that the moment our hearts are emptied of selfishness and ambition and self-seeking and everything that is contrary to God's law, the Holy Spirit will come and fill every corner of our hearts. But if we are full of pride and conceit and ambition and the world, there is no room for the Spirit of God. Before we pray that God would fill us, I believe we ought to pray that He would empty us.”

“The Spirit of God first imparts love; He next inspires hope, and then gives liberty; and that is about the last thing we have in many of our churches.”

fields.title: A. R. Torrey (1856 – 1928)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Reuben Archer Torrey was born on 28 January 1856 in Hoboken, New Jersey. He was brilliantly educated, graduating from Yale University and then Yale Divinity School before pursuing further theological study at Leipzig and Erlangen universities in Germany. He came to genuine faith in Christ after a period of wrestling with doubt, and was subsequently baptised in the Holy Spirit in an experience that transformed his ministry.

In 1889, D. L. Moody invited Torrey to become the first superintendent of what would become Moody Bible Institute in Chicago. Torrey served alongside Moody faithfully, and when Moody died in 1899, Torrey stepped in to the role of the world’s foremost evangelical leader. He also became pastor of Moody Church.

From 1902 to 1907, Torrey conducted extraordinary evangelistic campaigns around the world, seeing tens of thousands of people come to Christ in Australia, New Zealand, India, China, Britain, and the United States. The Australian revival of 1902 – 1903 alone saw an estimated one hundred thousand converts across the major cities.

Torrey later became Dean of what is now Biola University in Los Angeles and pastor of the Church of the Open Door. He wrote more than forty books, with How to Pray and The Power of Prayer remaining his best-loved works. He died on 26 October 1928, having spent his life training the church in the theology and practice of Spirit-empowered prayer.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The Australian revival of 1902 stands as the crowning answer to prayer in Torrey’s life. Before the campaign began, Torrey and his team spent months in sustained prayer, crying out to God for a genuine work of the Spirit. They refused to move until they had confidence that God had heard.

When the meetings opened in Melbourne, the results were staggering. Churches were overflowing. Hardened men broke down in tears. Whole families were converted in a single service. The local newspapers — not known for sympathy to the church — reported the extraordinary scenes. In Sydney, Brisbane, Auckland, and other cities, the same wave of blessing swept through. Torrey estimated over one hundred thousand genuine conversions in the campaign. He attributed every single one to prayer: prayer before the campaign, prayer during the meetings, and prayer by faithful intercessors in the background.

Torrey always taught that the decisive difference in any ministry was not the preacher’s talent but the chu rch’s prayer: “When the devil sees a man or woman who really believes in prayer, who knows how to pray, and who really does pray, and above all, when he sees a whole church on its face before God in prayer, he trembles as much as he ever did, for he knows that his day in that church or community is at an end.”

Key Scriptures

James 5:16 — “The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.”

1 John 5:14 — “This is the confidence that we have toward Him, that if we ask anything according to His will He hears us.”

His Words on Prayer

“If we would pray aright, the first thi ng we should do is to see to it that we really get an audience with God, that we really get into His very presence. Before a word of petition is offered, we should have the definite consciousness that we are talking to God, and should believe that He is li stening and is going to grant the thing that we ask of Him.”

“We are too busy to pray, and so we are too busy to have power. We have a great deal of activity, but we accomplish little; many services, but few conversions; much machinery, but few results.”

“All that God is, and all that God has, is at the disposal of prayer. Prayer can do anything that God can do, and as God can do everything, prayer is omnipotent.”

“Oh, men and women, pray through; pray through! Do not just begin to pray and pray a little while and throw up your hands and quit; but pray and pray and pray until God bends the heavens and comes down.”

“Triumphant prayer is almost impossible where there is neglect of the study of the Word of God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Prayer that is b orn of meditation upon the Word of God is the prayer that soars upward most easily to God's listening ears.”

“If I am to have faith when I pray, I must find some promise in the Word of God to rest my faith on. The Bible is packed from beginning to end with divine promises. Lay hold of them and pray them back to God.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Getting into God's presence is only possible by the Holy Spirit's power, so we should look to the Holy Spirit to really lead us into the presence of God, and should not be hasty in words until He has actually brought us there.”

“The Spirit, when He prays through us, or helps us to meet the mighty “oughtness” of right praying, trims our praying down to the will of God.”

“We must know the power of the Blood if we a re to know the power of God. Our knowing experimentally the power of the Word, the power of the Holy Spirit, and the power of prayer is dependent upon our knowing the power of the Blood of Christ.”

fields.title: E. M. Bounds (1835 – 1913)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Edward McKendree Bounds was born on 15 August 1835 in Shelby County, Missouri. He trained as a lawyer and was admitted to the bar at the age of nineteen, but within a few years felt the call of God so powerfully that he left his legal career and entered the Methodist ministry. He was a man of extraordinary zeal and dedication from the very beginning.

During the American Civil War, Bounds served as a Confederate Army chaplain. He was wounded in the First Battle of Franklin, Tennessee, and spent time as a prisoner of war. After the war, he returned to pastoral ministry, serving churches in Missouri, Alabama, and Tennessee. For eight years he served as the editor of the Christian Advocate newspaper in Nashville.

Bounds was not famous during his lifetime. He served in relative obscurity. But from the mid-1880s until his death in 1913, he rose every morning at four o'clock and prayed for three hours before the rest of the household woke. He did this every day for thirty years. He did not merely write about prayer — he lived it.

During those pre-dawn hours, Bounds also wrote. He produced eight manuscripts on the subject of prayer, covering its necessity, its power, its weapons, and its relation to the preacher and the church. None of these manuscripts were published during his lifetime. After his death on 24 August 1913, his friends gathered the manuscripts and published them. They have since sold millions of copies and remain among the most powerful and convicting writings on prayer in existence.

A Great Answer to Prayer

T he greatest answered prayer in E. M. Bounds’ life is the publication and global influence of his eight books on prayer — books he never saw published, written in the hidden hours of pre-dawn prayer.

Bounds prayed faithfully for thirty years in obscurity, believing that the Church desperately needed to be awakened to the power and necessity of prayer. He saw almost none of the fruit of his labours in his own lifetime. Yet God was listening. In the century following his death, his books have stirred millions of pastors and intercessors to give themselves to prayer, and their influence continues to grow.

This is itself one of the most powerful testimonies to the nature of answered prayer: that God sometimes answers our prayers not in our lifetime but through th e legacy we leave. Bounds’ prayer — that the Church would be revived through a deeper understanding of prayer — has been answered on a scale he could never have imagined.

Key Scriptures

Luke 18:1 — “Men always ought to pray and not lose heart.”

Ephesians 6:18 — “Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, being watchful to this end with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints.”

John 15:16 — “You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He may give it to you.”

“What the Church needs today is not more machinery or better, not new organisations or more and novel methods, but men whom the Holy Ghost can use — men of prayer, men mighty in prayer. “Prayers outlive the lives of t hose who uttered them; outlive a generation, outlive an age, outlive a world.”

“Around us is a world lost in sin, above us is a God willing and able to save; it is ours to build the bridge that links heaven and earth, and prayer is the mighty instrument that does the work.”

“Talking to men for God is a great thing, but talking to God for men is greater still.”

“Prayer is the easiest and hardest of all things; the simplest and the sublimest; the weakest and the most powerful; its results lie outside the range of human possibilities — they are limited only by the omnipotence of God.”

“The Word of God is the fulcrum upon which the lever of prayer is placed, and by which things are mightily moved. God speaks to man in the Bible; man speaks to God in prayer.

One reads the Bible to discover God's will; he prays in order that he may receive power to do that will.”

“The word of God is the food by which prayer is nourished and made strong. No two things are more essential to a Spirit-filled life than Bible-reading and secret prayer.”

“It is only when the whole heart is gripped with the passion of prayer that the life -giving fire descends, for none but the earnest man gets access to the ear of God.”

“Men whom the Holy Spirit can use — men of prayer, men mighty in prayer. The Holy Spirit does not come on machinery but on men. He does not anoint plans, but men — men of prayer.”

“Every mighty move of the Spirit of God has had its source in the prayer chamber.”

fields.title: Jonathan Edwards (1703 – 1758)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Jonathan Edwards was born on 5 October 1703 in East Windsor, Connecticut, into a family steeped in Puritan piety. His father was a pastor, his mother the daughter of the famous preacher Solomon Stoddard. Edwards entered Yale College at the age of thirteen and graduated at seventeen. After further study, he became his grandfather’s assistant at Northampton, Massachusetts, in 1727, and took sole charge of the congregation when Stoddard died in 1729.

Edwards was not merely a preacher — he was one of the greatest intellects in American history.

He read the philosophers Locke and Newton and brought their insights into conversation with Scripture, building a theology of remarkable depth and beauty. His favourite theme was the absolute majesty and sovereignty of God, and the total dependence of humanity on divine grace.

In 1734 – 35, a great revival broke out in Northampton under his ministry. More than 300 of the 1,100 inhabitants made professions of faith within six months. His report, A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God, sent shockwaves through America and England, helping to prepare the ground for the Great Awakening of 1740 – 42 — arguably the most significant spiritual awakening in American history.

In 1750, Edwards was controversially dismissed by his own congregation and spent seven years as a missionary among Native Americans in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. He was then invited to become President of Princeton College, but died of a smallpox inoculation just weeks after taking the post on 22 March 1758. He remains the greatest theologian America has ever produced, and his writings on revival, prayer, and the work of the Spirit are without equal.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The revival of 1734 – 35 in Northampton was the direct answer to years of prayer by a small congregation that refused to give up on God. Edwards himself described the spiritual state of the town before the revival as deeply discouraging — young people addicted to night-walking, tavern-drinking, and immorality; community leaders locked in bitter disputes; and the church small and ineffective.

Two untimely deaths in the spring of 1734 shocked the town into reflection. Simultaneously, Edwards began preaching with focused power on justification by faith alone. In December 1734, six young people were converted, including a young woman known as one of the greatest social butterflies in the whole town. Her radical transformation became the talk of the community.

Within six months, over 300 of the 1,100 people in Northampton — more than one in four — had been converted. The revival spread to neighbouring towns along the Connecticut River Valley. Edwards recorded: “God has also seemed to go out of His usual way in the quickness of His work, and the swift progress His Spirit has made in His operation, on the hearts of many.”

This was the answer to years of believing, persevering prayer.

Key Scriptures

Isaiah 44:3 — “I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and floods on the dry ground; I will pour M y Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring.”

2 Chronicles 7:14 — “If My people who are called by My name will humble themselves, and pray and seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, and will forgiv e their sin and heal their land.”

Philippians 4:6 — “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.”

His Words on Prayer

“The true spirit of prayer is no other than God' s own Spirit dwelling in the hearts of the saints. And as this spirit comes from God, so doth it naturally tend to God in holy breathings and pantings. It naturally leads to God, to converse with Him by prayer.”

“When God has something very great to accom plish for His Church, it is His will that there should precede it the extraordinary prayers of His people. When God is about to accomplish great things for His Church, He will begin by remarkably pouring out the spirit of grace and supplication.”

“There i s no way that Christians, in a private capacity, can do so much to promote the work of God and advance the kingdom of Christ as by prayer.”

“He that lives a prayerless life, lives without God in the world.”

“Prayer is as natural an expression of faith as breathing is to life.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“True religion disposes persons to be much alone in solitary places for holy meditation and prayer. It is the nature of true grace to delight in retirement and secret converse with God. A true Christian doubtless delights in religious fellowship, but he also delights at times to retire from all mankind, to converse with God in solitude.”

“It is God's will through His wonderful grace that the prayers of His saints should be one of the great principal means of carrying on the designs of Christ's kingdom in the world.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“The true spirit of prayer is no other than God's own Spirit dwelling in the hearts of the saints.”

“There is no spiritual awakening without the power of the Holy Spirit.”

“When God is about to do a mighty new thing, He always sets His people praying, and pours out the spirit of grace and supplication upon them as the first sign of what is coming.”

fields.title: Charles Finney (1792 – 1875)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Charles Grandison Finney was born on 29 August 1792 in Warren, Connecticut. He grew up on the American frontier in upstate New York, received little formal education, and trained as a lawyer. As he studied law, he noticed how often the legal textbooks quoted the Bible. He purchased a Bible to check the references — and the Bible captured him.

After months of wrestling with his soul, Finney surrendered to Christ on 10 October 1821 in a profound and transformative conversion experience in the woods near his home. That very e vening he was baptised with the Holy Spirit in an experience he described as “wave after wave of liquid love”. He immediately gave up his legal career and began preaching.

Finney was active as a revivalist from 1825 to 1835, and the results were extraordinary. Entire towns were turned upside down. Taverns were closed. Crime rates dropped. Social reform followed wherever he preached. His most famous campaign was in Rochester, New York, in 1830 – 31, where an estimated ten thousand people were converted and the whole character of the city was transformed.

In 1835, Finney joined the faculty of Oberlin College in Ohio, which was a pioneer in admitting both women and African Americans. He served as its second president from 1851 to 1865. He wrote the landmark Lectures on Revivals of Religion, which has inspired more revivals than almost any other book outside the Bible, and was used by God to ignite the Welsh Revival of the 1840s and many others. He died in 1875 at the age of 82 and is regarded as the Father of Modern Revivalism.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The Rochester revival of 1830 –31 remains the greatest single answered prayer in Finney’s ministry. Before the campaign, Finney’s intercessor — the remarkable “Father Nash” (Daniel Nash) — had gone ahead of him into the city days beforehand, renting a small dark room and spending entire days on his face before God, weeping, fasting, and crying out for souls.

When Finney arrived and began preaching, the Spirit of God moved with extraordinary power. A leading pastor who was converted in the Rochester meetings gave this account: “The whole community was stirred. Religion was the topic of conversation in the house, in the shop, in the office and on the street. The only theatre in the city was converted into a livery stable; the only circus into a soap and candle factory. Rum shops were closed; the Sabbath was honoured; the sanctuaries were thronged with happy worshippers.”

Over ten thousand people were genuinely converted in that one campaign. Finney himself attributed everything to prayer — Father Nash’s hidden intercessions, the prayer of local believers, and the earnest preparation of his own heart before he ever opened his mouth to preach.

Key Scriptures

Luke 11:13 — “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”

Isaiah 44:3 — “I will pour My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring.”

Acts 2:17 — “In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams.”

His Words on Prayer

“A revival may be expected when Christians have a spirit of prayer for a revival — when they pray as if their hearts were set upon it; when they go about groaning out their heart's desire; when they have real travail of soul.”

“Nothing tends more to cement the hearts of Christians than praying together. Never do they love one another so well as when they witness the outpouring of each other's hearts in prayer.”

“It was very common to find Christians, whenever they met in any place, instead of engaging in conversation, to fall on their knees in prayer.”

“What are our Bibles good for, if we do not lay hold on their precious promises, and use them as the ground of our faith when we pray for the blessing of God?”

“If you find yourself strongly drawn to desire a blessing, you are to understand it as an intimation that God is willing to bestow that particular blessing, and so you are bound to believe it.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“God says He is more ready to give His Holy Spirit to them that ask Him than parents are to give bread to their children. Here we are bound to believe that we shall receive it when we pray for it. You have no right to put in an “if” and say, “Lord, if it be Thy will, give us Thy Holy Spirit.” This is to insult God.”

“Prayer is an essential link in the chain of causes that lead to a revival. Truth by itself will never produce the effect without the Spirit of God, and that Spirit is given in answer to prayer.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Be filled with His Spirit, and He will give you objects enough to pray for. He will give you as much of the spirit of prayer as you have strength of body to bear.”

“But as I turned and was about to take a seat by the fire, I received a mighty baptism of the Holy Ghost. Without any expectation of it, without ever having the thought in my mind that there was any such thing for me, the Holy Spirit descended upon me in a manner that seemed to go through me, body and soul. I could feel the impression, like a wave of electricity, going through and through me. Indeed it seemed to come in waves and waves of liquid love.”

“Prayer is not the foe to work, it doe s not paralyse activity. It works mightily; prayer itself is the greatest work.”

fields.title: Rees Howells (1879 – 1950)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Rees Howells was born in 1879 in the small coal-mining village of Brynamman in South Wales.

He grew up in a working-class Welsh family and as a young man emigrated to the United States, where he contracted typhoid fever and, near death, made a promise to God: “If you let me live, I will give you my life.” He recovered, returned to Wales, and was swept into the Welsh Revival of 1904 – 1905 under Evan Roberts.

Following his radical conversion and a deeper consecration of himself to God, Howells entered a remarkable journey in which the Holy Spirit began to teach him what he called “true intercession” — prayer involving identification with the need, agony of soul, and the gaining of spiritual authority. He tested these principles first in local ministry and then as a missionary in South Africa, where revival accompanied his work.

In 1924, Howells founded the Bible College of Wales in Swansea, which became a centre of prayer and intercession. The college trained missionaries and sent them to the nations, living entirely by faith. During the years leading up to World War II, Howells became increasingly burdened for world events and shifted his intercession from local concerns to national and international affairs.

During World War II (1939 – 1945), Howells and his college community prayed every evening from 7 p.m. to midnight, plus additional hours in the morning. They interceded specifically for key turning points in the war — Dunkirk, the Battle of Britain, North Africa, and others. Many believe their intercessions were decisive in those moments. Rees Howells died in February 1950, and his biography, Rees Howells: Intercessor by Norman Grubb, has since inspired generations of intercessors worldwide.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Of all the answered prayers in Howells’ life, none is more dramatic than the evacuation of Dunkirk in May 1940. As Hitler’s armies drove the Allied forces back to the b eaches of northern France, over 300,000 British and French soldiers were trapped, with the German tanks closing in.

Invasion of Britain seemed certain.

On 21 May 1940, Howells wrote in his diary: “The situation looked extremely black for Britain.

It was an hour of near panic.” He and his college community cried out to God with agonising intercession. On 28 May, as the prayer warriors prayed together, a deep peace settled over them.

One student prayed at the end of the meeting: “I feel sure something has happened.”

On 29 May, the evacuation of Dunkirk began. Inexplicably, on 23 May, the German High Command had issued a halt order for all ground troops — an order that remains unexplained by military historians to this day. At the same time, the English Channel, normally rough, fell to an extraordinary calm, allowing small civilian boats to cross and bring the soldiers home. Over 338,000 men were rescued. Air Chief Marshal Lord Dowding, Commander of Fighter Command, later said: “Even during the battle one realis ed from day to day how much external support was coming in. At the end of the battle one had the sort of feeling that there had been some special Divine intervention.” Rees Howells believed it was the direct answer to prayer.

Key Scriptures

Isaiah 62:6 – 7 — “You who make mention of the LORD, do not keep silent, and give Him no rest till He establishes and till He makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

Ezekiel 22:30 — “I sought for a man among them who would make a wall, and stand in the gap before Me on b ehalf of the land, that I should not destroy it; but I found no one.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.”

His Words on Prayer

“There are three things to be seen in an intercessor which are not necessarily found in ordinary prayer: identification, agony, and authority.”

“The intercessor must become responsible for the prayer that the Holy Spirit gives them.

They must “pray through” until the prayer is answered.”

“Before God will use you in intercession, it will cost you. The intercessors love God so much that they want to obey. They will pay the price because of their love for the Saviour.”

“Once the Holy Spirit has called an intercessor to a spiritual conflict, the intercessor must carry on to completing the task, no matter what the cost — and it will be costly.”

“Prayer is not an exercise, it is the life.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“The path of the intercessor i s the way of the cross. It is also the way of fellowship with Jesus on a very deep level. It is a sacrifice of love. The intercessor has the sentence of death — death to self — in himself.”

“As the crucifixion of self proceeds, intercession begins. You ar e never forced into prayer. The intercessor needs to be willing to enter into a new place of intercession with God.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“The intercessor must become responsible for the prayer that the Holy Spirit gives them.”

“As their prayers gr ew more fervent, they also felt the increasing presence of the Holy Spirit among them. The Spirit was the engine of all true intercession.”

“God help us to know the Spirit and to reverence Him as the Spirit of prayer!”

fields.title: Billy Graham (1918 – 2018)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

William Franklin Graham Jr. was born on 7 November 1918 on a dairy farm near Charlotte, North Carolina. He grew up during the Great Depression, learning the value of hard work and a simple faith. In the autumn of 1934, at the age of fifteen, he attended a series of revival meetings led by the travelling evangelist Mordecai Ham. One evening, under deep conviction, he walked to the front and gave his life to Christ.

After attending Bob Jones College, the Florida Bible Institute, and Wheaton College (where he met his future wife Ruth Bell, daughter of medical missionaries to China), Graham was ordained and began pastoral work. In 1945 he joined Youth for Christ and began preaching at rallies across America and in postwar Europe.

In September 1949, Graham opened a series of revival meetings in Los Angeles. Planned for three weeks, the tent meetings were extended to eight weeks as the city was gripped by what newspapers called the greatest religious revival in the history of Southern California. Over 350,000 attended, and 3,000 publicly committed their lives to Christ. Almost overnight, Billy Graham became a national figure.

Over the following six decades, Graham preached the Gospel in live crusades to an estimated 215 million people in 185 countries, with many millions more reached through radio, television, and film. He counselled twelve US presidents. He was the first major evangelist to insist on racially integrated crusades in the American South. The Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, which he founded in 1950, continues its work around the world. Graham died at his home in Montreat, North Carolina, on 21 February 2018, at the age of 99.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The Los Angeles crusade of 1949 was born out of extraordinary prayer. A cross-denominational revival prayer network with over one hundred and twenty clergy had been meeting and praying for a city-wide awakening for months before Graham arrived. More than one thousand prayer groups across Los Angeles were interceding specifically for the crusade.

In the months before the crusade opened, Graham himself had retreated to the San Bernardino mountains in a personal crisis of faith — wrestling with intellectual doubts about the Bible. On his knees before God, he placed his open Bible on a tr ee stump and said, in essence, “Lord, I cannot answer all the questions. But I accept this Book as Your Word by faith.” A deep peace settled over him. He arose and went to preach.

The results surpassed all expectation. Country music star Stuart Hamblen was converted and his changed life became front-page news. When media magnate William Randolph Hearst — for reasons no one has fully explained — sent the telegram to all his editors “Puff Graham,” the crusade exploded into national prominence overnight. Thousands came to faith in those eight weeks. Graham always said it was entirely the work of prayer.

Key Scriptures

Romans 10:14 — “How then shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed?

And how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?”

2 Timothy 4:2 — “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; correct, rebuke and encourage — with great patience and careful instruction.”

John 3:16 — “For God so loved the world that He gave His onl y Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is for every moment of our lives, not just for times of suffering or joy. Prayer is really a place, a place where you meet God in genuine conversation.”

“In the Bible God speaks to us; in prayer we speak to God. Both are essential.”

“You cannot pray for someone and hate them at the same time.”

“True prayer is a way of life, not just for use in cases of emergency. Make it a habit, and when the need a rises you will be in practice.”

“Heaven is full of answers to prayer for which no one ever bothered to ask.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Pray frequently as you read the Bible and you will discover a fellowship with God.

Prayer and Bible study are inseparably linked. Effective prayer is born out of the prompting of God's Spirit as we read His Word.”

“The Spirit of God takes the Word of God and makes the child of God. Read your Bible daily. Do not be content to skim through a chapter merely to satisfy your conscience.

Hide the Word of God in your heart. It comforts, guides, corrects, encourages — all we need is there.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Rely constantly on the Holy Spirit. We know that the Holy Spirit prays for us, and what a comfort that should be to the weakest of us. Stand aside and let Him take over all the choices and decisions of your life.”

“The Spirit -filled life is not abnormal; it is the normal Christian life. Anything less is subnormal; it is less than what God wants and provides for His children.”

“It is never a question of how much you and I have of the Spirit, but how much He has of us.”

fields.title: Henry Blackaby (1935 – 2024)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Henry Thomas Blackaby was born on 15 April 1935 in Williams Lake, British Columbia, Canada. H e earned his bachelor’s degree in history and English from the University of British Columbia and his theological degrees from Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary in California. He served as a music director, education director, and pastor in California before answering a very specific call that changed his life.

In 1970, a Canadian pastor approached Blackaby with a challenge: “The only hope for Canada is if Canadian pastors come back home.” Blackaby heard this as a word from God. He and his wife Marilynn moved to Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, to pastor Faith Baptist Church — a tiny, dying congregation of ten people.

What happened over the next twelve years was nothing short of miraculous. The church grew dramatically, planted thirty-eight daughter churches and mission posts, and became the epicentre of the remarkable Saskatoon Revival of 1971 — a city-wide awakening that transformed entire denominations. During those years, Blackaby developed the principles that would become Experiencing God.

His book Experiencing God: Knowing and Doing the Will of God, co-written with his son Richard and Claude King in 1990, has sold over seven million copies and been translated into more than forty-five languages. It has been described as one of the most influential Christian books of the twentieth century. Blackaby went on to serve the Southern Baptist Convention's Home Mission Board as Director of Prayer and Spiritual Awakening, travelling the world to call the Church back to God. He died on 10 February 2024 at the age of 88.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Before the Saskatoon Revival of 1971 broke out, Henry Blackaby and a group of Saskatoon pastors had been meeting together every week for two years, praying specifically for God to send revival to their city. They had no guarantee that anything would happen. But they prayed and they waited.

On 13 October 1971, twin evangelists Ralph and Lou Sutera arrived for what was planned as a week-and-a-half of meetings at Ebenezer Baptist Church. But God had different plans. Within days, the meetings could not be contained. The congregation moved to a larger church, and that was overflowed in two nights. They moved to the largest church in the city — 1,600 seats — and ran double services nightly. Finally, the Saskatoon Centennial Auditorium was rented, with 2,400 seats, and still it was full.

Entire denominations were transformed. The Christian Missionary and Alliance denomination reported a one hundred percent increase in conversions in that first year. Baptised church members discovered they had never been truly born again. Families were reconciled. Debts were paid. Enemies were forgiven. Blackaby said that the entire DNA of his life was changed during the revival — and the principles he lived through those days became the message he spent the rest of his life proclaiming to the world.

Key Scriptures

Jeremiah 29:13 — “You will seek Me and find Me, when you seek Me with all your heart.”

John 14:21 — “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves Me.

And he who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and manifest Myself to him.”

Isaiah 55:8 – 9 — “My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is designed to adjust you to God's will, not to adjust God to your will.”

“All revival begins, and continues, in the prayer meeting. In times of revival, thousands may be found on their knees for hours, lifting up their heartfelt cries, with thanksgiving, to heaven.”

“Prayer is a relationship, not a religious activity.”

“When God answers your prayer, He receives the glory, your faith is increased, and you have a fresh experience of Hi s love.”

“Prayerless leaders are like ship captains without compasses; they can make their best guess at which direction to go, but they have no assurance they are heading the right way. Prayer keeps leaders focused on the one absolutely consistent factor in life — God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“God speaks by the Holy Spirit through the Bible, prayer, circumstances, and the church to reveal Himself, His purposes, and His ways. If you have trouble hearing God speak, you are in trouble at the very heart of your Christian experience.”

“When you want to know how God wants you to reach your city, or be involved in His work, ask Him. His promise is to always answer when we pray according to His will.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“God speaks by the Holy Spiri t through the Bible, prayer, circumstances, and the church to reveal Himself, His purposes, and His ways.”

“Prayer is not solely about making requests, but about aligning our desires with God's plans for us. The Spirit prompts us to seek out what God has in store.”

“Revival is a divinely initiated work in which God's people pray, repent of their sin, and return to a holy, Spirit-filled, obedient, love-relationship with God.”

fields.title: Bill Bright (1921 – 2003)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

William R. Bright was born on 19 October 1921 in Coweta, Oklahoma, the sixth of seven children of a cattle-ranching family. Until eighth grade he attended school in a one-room schoolhouse. After distinguished academic achievement at Northeastern State University, he moved to California and built a successful confections business. He was introduced to the Gospel through the ministry of Henrietta Mears at Hollywood Presbyterian Church, and in 1945 surrendered his life completely to Christ.

While studying at Princeton and Fuller theological seminaries, Bright felt an overwhelming call from God. He and his wife Vonette signed what they called a “slave contract” — literally a written surrender of all their rights and ambitions to Jesus — and in 1951 launched Campus Crusade for Christ at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Within months, hundreds of students at UCLA had given their lives to Christ, including the student body president, the campus newspaper editor, and several athletes. By the end of the 1950s, Campus Crusade had spread to dozens of campuses. The ministry grew to become one of the largest Christian organisations in the world, with 26,000 staff and 225,000 volunteers in 191 countries.

In 1952, Bright wrote The Four Spiritual Laws — a simple gospel presentation that has been distributed to over 2.5 billion people. In 1979, he produced the Jesus film, which by his death had been translated into over 1,400 languages and viewed by more than five billion people. In 1996 he received the Templeton Prize for Progress in Religion — worth $1.1 million — and donated the entire sum to promote prayer and fasting. Bill Bright died on 19 July 2003.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The campus breakthrough at UCLA in 1951 was the seed from which everything else in Bright's ministry grew. It was entirely the product of prayer. When Bright launched Campus Crusade with a handful of volunteers, there was no precedent for this kind of student ministry and no guarantee of success. He and Vonette prayed earnestly before every meeting, every conversation, every outreach.

Within months, the student body president of UCLA, the campus newspaper editor, and several top athletes had committed their lives to Christ. The transformation of these high-profile students sent shockwaves through the campus. Word spread. The movement grew. Within a decade it had become a national and then international force.

But the greatest answered prayer in Bright's life was the Jesus film. It took years of prayer, fund-raising by faith, theological preparation, and logistical work to produce. When it was released in 1979, it was initially shown in just a few countries. Bright prayed that it would reach the world.

Over the following decades, God answered that prayer far beyond what Bright could have imagined: the film has now been seen by more than five billion people in over 200 countries, and hundreds of millions of people have prayed the prayer of salvation after watching it. It is the most watched film in human history.

Key Scriptures

Matthew 28:19 – 20 — “Go therefore and make discip les of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you.”

Acts 1:8 — “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

1 John 5:14 – 15 — “This is the confidence that we have toward Him, that if we ask anything according to His will He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of Him.”

His Words on Prayer

“Show me a church or a Christian organisation that emphasises prayer, and I'll show you a ministry where people are excited about Jesus Christ and are witnessing for Hi m.”

“I believe the power of fasting as it relates to prayer is the spiritual atomic bomb that our Lord has given us to destroy the strongholds of evil and usher in a great revival and spiritual harvest around the world.”

“Fasting with a pure heart and mo tives brings personal revival and adds power to our prayers. Personal revival occurs because fasting is an act of humility.”

“Fasting and prayer can bring about a change in the direction of our nation, the nations of the earth, and the fulfilment of the G reat Commission.”

“Not only do you have the ear of the greatest Person in the universe, but as you kneel in your place of prayer, you have the privilege of being used of God to help change the lives of individuals and nations.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“His promise is that He will always answer when we pray according to His will: “This is the confidence which we have before Him, that, if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14–15). Lay hold of this promise and pray accordingly.”

“Fasting and prayer are the only disciplines that fulfil the requirements of 2 Chronicles 7:14: “If My people who are called by My name will humble themselves, and pray and seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven.””

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Fasting reduces the power of self so that the Holy Spirit can do a more intense work within us.”

“We are filled with the Holy Spirit by faith alone. Pray: “Dear Father, I need You. Fill me with the Holy Spirit as You commanded me to be filled and as You promised in Your Word that You would do if I asked in faith.””

“Through fasting and prayer, the Holy Spirit can transform your life. Fasting and prayer can effect change on a much grander scale when God's people seek His face with broken and repentant hearts.”

fields.title: Loren Cunningham (1935 – 2023)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Loren Duane Cunningham was born on 30 June 1935 in the oil boom town of Taft, California, into a family with generations of Christian ministers. From early childhood, prayer and faith were woven into the fabric of his life. His parents were Assemblies of God ministers who modelled radical trust in God.

In June 1956, at the age of twenty, Cunningham was kneeling in prayer in a missionary’s home in the Bahamas, asking God for a message to preach that evening, when he received a remarkable vision. He saw a map of the world come alive, with waves crashing on the continents and turning into young people — thousands upon thousands of young men and women from every nation, going to every nation, preaching the Gospel. He had no idea how to interpret it or what to do with it, but he wrote it down.

Four years later, in 1960, Cunningham founded Youth With A Mission (YWAM) in Lausanne, Switzerland, at the age of twenty-four, with his wife Darlene. YWAM broke the mould of 1960s missions by welcoming young people who were not career missionaries to serve short-term, unsalaried, interdenominationally, on any continent. The movement grew with remarkable speed.

In 1978, Cunningham co-founded the University of the Nations in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. By the time of his death on 6 October 2023 at the age of 88, YWAM had grown to over 20,000 full-time staff from more than 150 nations serving at over 2,000 locations in 191 countries. Cunningham was the first person in history to travel for the sake of the Gospel to every sovereign nation, dependent country, and more than 100 territories on earth.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Shortly after founding YWAM, Cunningham needed a farm to serve as the first permanent base for the growing ministry. He had no money, no donor, and no realistic prospects. He did what he always did: he prayed. Then, in an act of bold faith, he went to an auction and bought a barbed wire, a milk can, and a hay wagon — farm items — before the farm existed.

His young students were bewildered. “What are these for?” they asked. “God is going to give us a farm for YWAM,” he replied simply. Shortly after, a man came to Cunningham and said three words: “I want to give you a farm.” It was exactl y the farm they needed. That farm became the mother base of the entire global movement, and it all began in prayer and faith.

But the greatest answered prayer in Cunningham’s life was the fulfilment of the 1956 vision itself. He spent sixty-seven years watching that vision come true — wave after wave of young people from every nation going to every nation with the Gospel of Christ. He saw millions of young people mobilised for missions through YWAM, and he died knowing that the vision was still unfolding.

Key Scriptures

Mark 16:15 — “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.”

John 10:27 — “My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.”

Acts 13:2 — “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.””

His Words on Prayer

“Hearing God is not all that difficult. If we know the Lord, we have already heard His voice — after all, it was the inner leading that brought us to Him in the first place. But we can hear His voice and still miss His best if we don't keep on listening.”

“Guidance is first of all a relationship with the Guide.”

“We get caught in our boxes — but when we pray outside of them, ask God, the impossible CAN be d one.”

“We followed the Three Steps to Hearing God: First, we took Christ's authority to silence the enemy. Second, we asked the Lord to clear from our minds any presumptions and preconceived ideas. Third, we waited, believing He would speak in the way and in the time that He chose.”

“The Lord will lead us into victory, but success itself is the most dangerous obstacle to properly hearing the voice of God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“When a critical mass of people have the Bible and apply what it teaches in their lives, a nation is transformed. The Book is the key to everything.”

“This is what hearing God is all about — getting to know Him better. Prayer is not primarily a technique for getting things; it is the language of relationship with the Father.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Every great historical move of the Spirit I had studied began with times of confession and deep repentance. God's power is released after a time of cleansing.”

“Whenever we came to a crossroads in the mission, we prayed until the Holy Spirit spoke. Then we obeyed. That is the only way to build anything that will last.”

“To know God and to make Him known — that is YWAM's call. And to know God, you must pray.”
