fields.title: Derek Prince (1915 – 2003)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Derek Prince was born in Bangalore, India, in 1915, to British parents. He was educated at the elite Eton College and then Cambridge University, where he was elected to a prestigious fellowship at King's College for his philosophical dissertation at the age of twenty-four. He described himself at the time as an atheist.

When World War II broke out, Prince joined the Royal Army Medical Corps as a conscientious objector. As a self-assigned philosophical exercise, he began to read the Bible. In 1941, while stationed in a milit ary barracks, he had what he described as a “supernatural experience” — a meeting with Jesus Christ. He later wrote: “Out of this encounter I formed two conclusions: first, that Jesus Christ is alive; second, that the Bible is a true, relevant, up-to-date book. These conclusions altered the whole course of my life.” Two weeks later he was baptised in the Holy Spirit.

The morning after his conversion, the man who had never prayed in his life could not stop praying. He was posted to North Africa and Palestine, where during his wartime service he met Lydia Christiansen, a Danish woman running an orphanage for eight girls in Ramallah. They married in 1946, and Prince instantly became the father of eight daughters. He gave up his Cambridge fellowship, was ordained, and founded a Pentecostal church in London.

From London, the Princes moved to Kenya, where Prince led a school and planted churches. He subsequently moved to the United States and Canada, eventually settling in Jerusalem in 1981 — a city he loved with a profound biblical conviction. He wrote over fifty books and 600 audio teachings, translated into more than 100 languages. He died in Jerusalem on 24 September 2003, one of the most widely-heard Bible teachers of the twentieth century.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The most dramatic answered prayer in Derek Prince’s life was his own conversion — an unsolicited, unexpected encounter with the living Christ while reading the Bible alone in a dark army barracks. Prince had not been seeking God. He had been studying the Bible as a philosopher studies an ancient text. But God broke through, and the man who had gone to sleep as an atheist woke up as a believer.

Prince often spoke of his grandmother, who had prayed for him faithfully throughout his irreligious years at university. He believed with absolute conviction that her years of prayer for him had prepared the ground for that extraordinary encounter.

Later in his ministry, while serving as a school principal in Kenya in the late 1950s, Prince prayed for people to be raised from the dead on two separate occasions — and both times God answered. These experiences deepened his understanding of the authority available to believers in prayer. He spent the remainder of his life teaching believers that prayer is not a religious formality but a weapon of war, a tool of healing, and a means of advancing the Kingdom of God on earth.

Key Scriptures

Ephesians 6:17 – 18 — “Take the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication.”

Romans 8:34 — “Christ Jesus who died — more than that, who was raised to life — is at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us.”

1 Timothy 2:1 — “I urge, then, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving be made for all people — for kings and all those in authority.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is limitless. It's our intercontinental ballistic missile. We can launch it from anywhere and make it reach anywhere.”

“The people who really rule the world are those who know how to pray.”

“Truth is not obtained cheaply. It demands much time given to prayer and study of the Scriptures, followed by practical application in our daily lives.”

“What kind of spiritual sacrifices does God expect us to offer? Ju st as Jesus offered up prayers and petitions during His life on earth, so should we. When we learn to pray, then we are qualified to rule.”

“If you are praying in faith, you say: “The answer is ten years nearer than when I started praying.””

Prayer and the Word of God

“The great revelation of the will of God is the Word of God. And the Word of God is packed from beginning to end with divine promises. The will of God is not hidden from us — it is revealed in Scripture. Pray the promises.”

“God has provide d us three main spiritual weapons: the Word of God, the name of Jesus, and the blood of Jesus. We launch these weapons through prayer, praise, preaching, and testimony.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“We cannot effectively serve God without the Holy Spirit.”

“Fasting deals with the two great barriers to the Holy Spirit that are erected by man's carnal nature — the stubborn self-will of the soul and the insistent self-gratifying appetites of the body.”

“The night before my conversion I hadn't known how to pr ay. The next day I couldn't stop praying. Even if I got a mug of water I had to pause and thank God for the water before I could drink it. Prayer was now as natural as breathing. That is the work of the Holy Spirit.”

fields.title: Timothy Keller (1950 – 2023)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Timothy James Keller was born on 23 September 1950 in Allentown, Pennsylvania. He grew up in a Lutheran family but did not come to a living faith until his time at Bucknell University in the late 1960s, where he became a Christian through involvement with InterVarsity Christian Fellowship. He went on to earn his Master of Divinity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary and his Doctor of Ministry at Westminster Theological Seminary.

Ordained in the Presbyterian Church of America, Keller served for nine years as pastor of West Hopewell Presbyterian Church in Hopewell, Virginia, before joining the faculty of Westminster Theological Seminary as Professor of Practical Theology. In 1989, against almost all human advice, he and his wife Kathy moved to New York City in response to a call from their denomination to plant a church in Manhattan.

Redeemer Presbyterian Church began with fewer than fifty people meeting in borrowed space.

Within a decade it had grown to thousands of weekly worshippers. By the time Keller retired as senior pastor in 2017, Redeemer drew over 5,000 people each Sunday to multiple services, had planted over one hundred churches in the New York metropolitan area, and had become a model of urban church ministry studied by pastors worldwide.

Keller’s books — including The Reason for God, The Prodigal God, and Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God — have sold millions of copies and been translated into scores of languages. He co-founded The Gospel Coalition and Redeemer City to City, which has trained church planters in global cities on every continent. In 2020 Keller was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, which he faced with extraordinary faith and transparency. He died on 19 May 2023, aged 72.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The planting and growth of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan is, by almost any measure, a remarkable answer to prayer. In 1989, New York City was not considered fertile ground for evangelical Christianity. The culture was aggressively secular, the pace of life brutally relentless, and the social pressure against religious commitment intense. Most church planting attempts in Manhattan had failed or remained tiny.

Keller and his wife prayed, studied, and prepared for years before moving to the city. They approached the task with theological rigour and cultural intelligence, trusting God to open hearts in what seemed like the hardest soil in America. God answered abundantly. The church grew from fifty to five hundred to five thousand — drawing young professionals, artists, academics, and sceptics who were encountering the Gospel perhaps for the first time.

Keller also testified that his battle with cancer, rather than destroying his prayer life, deepened and transformed it. He wrote that facing death forced him to be still before God in a way his busy ministry had never permitted. The cancer taught him that prayer is not a technique for getting results but an encounter with the living God in which the soul is remade. He faced his final years with a joy and confidence that many who knew him described as one of the most powerful testimonies they had ever witnessed.

Key Scriptures

Matthew 6:6 — “When you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in s ecret will reward you.”

Philippians 4:6 – 7 — “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is awe, intimacy, struggle — yet the way to reality. There is nothing more important, or harder, or richer, or more life-altering. There is absolutely nothing so great as prayer.”

“Prayer is the only entryway into genuine self -knowledge. It is also the main way we experience deep change — the reordering of our loves. Prayer is how God gives us so many of the unimaginable things He has for us. It is the way we know God, the way we finally treat God as God. Prayer is simply the key to everything we need to do and be in life.”

“We know God will answer us when we call because one terrible day He did not answer Jesus when He called. Jesus’ prayers were given the rejection that we sinners merit so that our prayers could have the reception that He merits.”

“Prayer is th e way to experience a powerful confidence that God is handling our lives well — that our bad things will turn out for good, our good things cannot be taken from us, and the best things are yet to come.”

“To fail to pray, then, is not to merely break some religious rule — it is a failure to treat God as God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Our prayers should arise out of immersion in the Scripture. We should plunge ourselves into the sea of God's language, the Bible. Listen, study, think, reflect, and ponder the Scriptures until there is an answering response in your heart — and then that response, offered back to God, is truly prayer.”

“What is essential in prayer is not that we learn to express ourselves, but that we learn to answer God. Real prayer begins when God speaks first — in His Word, through His Spirit — and we respond.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Prayer is continuing a conversation that God has started through His Word and His grace, which eventually becomes a full encounter with Him.”

“A triun e God would call us to converse with Him, because He wants to share the joy He has always had within Himself. Prayer is our way of entering into the happiness of God Himself.”

“Prayer turns theology into experience. The doctrines of Scripture must become the fuel for prayer, or they will merely remain knowledge in the head. When the Spirit takes truth and drives it into prayer, the fire is lit.”

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
What These Men Leave to Us

You have now walked through the lives of fifteen men who prayed. They came from different centuries, different continents, different denominations, and different backgrounds. Some were scholars and some were uneducated. Some pastored great churches and some served in obscurity.

Some are celebrated names in church history and some are known only to those who search deeply for the hidden heroes of the faith. But every single one of them discovered the same truth: that prayer is not one activity among many, but the foundation on which all genuine ministry is built.

Look at what prayer did in their lives. It brought the revival Andrew Murray's father had prayed for over thirty years. It filled D. L. Moody with the power of the Holy Spirit on a New York street and sent him to preach to millions. It turned the tide of World War II through a small company of intercessors in a Welsh Bible College. It planted a church in the hardest city in America and grew it to five thousand people. It brought rain to a remote Chinese island when an idol's followers challenged the living God. It converted a Cambridge atheist through a Bible read alone in an army barracks. It turned a dying congregation of ten people in the Canadian prairies into a church that planted thirty-eight daughters.

Prayer works. Not as a magic formula. Not as a technique. Not as a religious duty performed to earn God's favour. Prayer works because God is real, God is present, God is listening, and God is powerful. Prayer works because Jesus Christ is at the right hand of the Father, ever living to make intercession for us (Heb rews 7:25). Prayer works because the Holy Spirit within us “helps our weakness” and “intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). When we pray, we are not speaking into an empty sky. We are speaking to the Creator and Sustainer of the universe, the One who holds every nation in the palm of His hand, the One who loved us enough to send His only Son to die for us.

The Common Thread

Looking at these fifteen men together, several patterns emerge that are worth naming.

First: they were all men of the Word. Not one of them prayed in isolation from Scripture.

Andrew Murray insisted that the Word and the Spirit must be united in prayer. E. M. Bounds declared that the Word of God is “the food by which prayer is nourished and made strong.” A. R .

Torrey taught that “prayer that is born of meditation upon the Word of God is the prayer that soars upward most easily to God's listening ears.” Timothy Keller described prayer as “continuing a conversation that God has started through His Word.” For all fifteen men, the Bible was not separate from prayer — it was the language of prayer, the fuel of prayer, and the foundation of prayer.

Second: they were all men who depended on the Holy Spirit. They did not trust in their own eloquence, their theological training, their organisational ability, or their natural gifts. Spurgeon said, “Prayer is the creation of the Holy Spirit.” Moody prayed until God came and overwhelmed him on a New York street. Torrey taught that entering God's presence is only possible by the Holy Spirit's power. Finney experienced the Spirit descending “in waves of liquid love.” Rees Howells spent his entire ministry under the direct guidance and anointing of the Holy Spirit. For all of these men, the Holy Spirit was not a doctrine to be discussed but a Person to be depended upon.

Third: they were all men who paid a price. Prayer is not easy. It is not convenient. It costs time, energy, sleep, comfort, and pride. E. M. Bounds rose at four in the morning every day for thirty years. Rees Howells and his community prayed every evening until midnight during the darkest years of the war. Andrew Murray lost his voice for two years in the crucible of surrender.

Watchman Nee spent twenty years in prison. Jonathan Edwards was dismissed by his own congregation. Charles Finney was mocked and opposed. Derek Prince gave up a brilliant academic career. Timothy Keller faced cancer with prayer as his only weapon. None of them told us prayer was easy. They told us it was worth it.

Fourth: they were all men whose prayers outlived them. The prayers of Andrew Murray's father for revival were answered in 1860, decades after those prayers began. E. M. Bounds’ prayer for a praying Church was answered through eight books published after his death. Rees Howells interceded for the State of Israel before it existed, and the nation was reborn in 1948, two years before he died. Loren Cunningham received a vision in prayer in 1956 that he spent sixty-seven years watching unfold. Billy Graham prayed for lost souls at every crusade, and the fruit of those prayers continued to ripple through individuals, families, and communities long after each meeting ended. Prayer is not limited by the lifetime of the one who prays. It reaches into eternity.

A Word to Ugandan Pastors

You are serving God in one of the most spiritually strategic places on earth. Uganda sits at the heart of the African continent, a nation with a history of Christian martyrdom, revival, and the extraordinary blessing of the Holy Spirit. The missionaries who came to Uganda in the nineteenth century paid a tremendous price. The Uganda Martyrs died with the name of Christ on their lips. The East African Revival of the twentieth century sent waves of Holy Spirit power through Uganda and beyond. You are the heirs of all of that.

But the inheritance of the past is not enough. Every generation must meet God afresh. The fire on the altar must be renewed every morning. And in your generation, the challenges are great: poverty and suffering among your people, family breakdown, political pressure, false teaching, spiritual warfare, the pull of material prosperity and personal ambition. Only a deep and sustained prayer life will equip you to face these challenges and lead your congregation through them.

You are also uniquely positioned for global influence. Uganda has given the world remarkable Christian leaders, preachers, and evangelists. Ugandan missionaries serve across Africa and beyond. Ugandan churches are sending churches. As you build your prayer life, you are not only serving your local congregation — you are building foundations for the global mission of the Church.

The fifteen men in this book were not super-humans. They were ordinary people who took God at His word. They prayed because they believed that God hears. They persisted because they believed that God answers. They sacrificed comfort and convenience because they believed that prayer is worth more than anything else they could do. Every one of them would say to you today: “You can do this. You must do this. The world you are trying to reach is waiting for you to pray.”

CALL TO ACTION A Charge to the Pastors and Teachers of Uganda

This book is not meant to sit on a shelf. It is meant to send you to your knees. As you close these pages, the question is not “What did I learn?” but “What will I do?”

Here are seven practical commitments you can make in response to what you have read: 1. Establish a Daily Prayer Appointment Every man in this book set aside specific time for prayer. Some prayed for hours each morning.

All of them were deliberate and disciplined. Choose a time — whether it is thirty minutes at dawn, an hour at midday, or an evening vigil — and protect it. Tell your family. Guard it from interruption. And keep it even on the days you do not feel like praying, for those are often the days your prayer matters most.

2. Ground Your Prayers in Scripture

As you pray, bring your Bible with you. Read a passage first. Let God speak before you speak.

Pray the promises back to God. Let the words of the Psalms become your own words. Let the prayers of Paul in Ephesians 1 and 3 shape the way you pray for your congregation. Let the great prayers of the Bible — Moses, Daniel, Nehemiah, Jesus — teach you what prayer looks like when it moves heaven.

3. Pray for the Filling of the Holy Spirit

Ask God every day for a fresh filling of the Holy Spirit. Not just for gifts and power — though those are real and important — but for the character of Christ to be formed in you. Ask the Spirit to show you what to pray for, to giv e you the burdens of God’s heart, and to intercede through you for the things that matter most to God.

4. Pray for Your Congregation by Name

Take a list of the people in your congregation and pray through it regularly. Pray for their marriages, their children, their work, their struggles, and their faith. When people bring you prayer requests, keep a record and follow up. Let your congregation know that you pray for them by name. This is one of the most powerful things a pastor can do.

5. Build a Culture of Prayer in Your Church

Spurgeon said the Monday evening prayer meeting was the engine of everything Metropolitan Tabernacle accomplished. Rees Howells’ prayer community gathered every evening. What is the prayer life of your congregation? Establish a regular prayer meeting. Teach on prayer from the pulpit. Share answered prayers publicly to build faith. Invite your elders and deacons to pray together before every meeting. Let prayer be the air your church breathes.

6. Find or Become a Prayer Partner

Almost every man in this book had people who prayed with and for him. Charles Finney had Father Nash. Loren Cunningham had a community of YWAM intercessors. Henry Blackaby had a group of Saskatoon pastors who prayed together for two years before the revival came. Find one or two other pastors or elders who will commit to pray with you regularly. And pray for one another specifically, honestly, and persistently.

7. Intercede for Uganda and the Nations

Your prayers are not limited to your congregation. The God you pray to is the God of the nations. Pray for Uganda — for its leaders, its families, its schools, its churches, its missionaries.

Pray for Africa. Pray for the unreached peoples of the earth. Pray for the coming of the Kingdom of God in every nation. As Rees Howells discovered, the scope of prayer is as wide as the heart of God.

A Final Word

Andrew Murray wrote: “The man who mobilises the Christian church to pray will make the greatest contribution to world evangelisation in history.”

E. M. Bounds declared : “Around us is a world lost in sin, above us is a God willing and able to save; it is ours to build the bridge that links heaven and earth, and prayer is the mighty instrument that does the work.”

Timothy Keller concluded: “There is absolutely nothing so great as prayer.”

These men were right. Prayer is the greatest work. It is the most important thing you will do today, and tomorrow, and every day of your ministry. It is the thing that makes everything else you do alive with the power of God. And it is available to you right now.

So close this book. Find a quiet place. Open your Bible. And pray. Not because you have to.

Because the God of Andrew Murray and Charles Spurgeon and Watchman Nee and D. L. Moody and all the rest — that same God — is waiting to meet you there.

“And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.”

Matthew 21:22 To God Alone Be the Glory
